## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
Session 3 of day 3, on the slope of the claim as a posterior distribution
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-85}
1. Priors and the posterior – what the priors imply before the data enter, the posterior of the two-way slope, and the checks of its computation
2. Persistence within countries – the posterior predictive check, and errors that persist from one year to the next
3. Partial pooling – a slope for each country, each estimated partly from the others
4. The result – the sensitivity to the priors, the slope across the models, and the probability of a negative slope
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave able to read a posterior distribution, to say what its priors imply, and to judge what a Bayesian model adds when 27 countries carry the evidence
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
The models were fitted once, with brms; you work in the workspace, in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.)
:::

::: notes
The third session goes back to the panel and estimates the slope of the claim by Bayesian methods. Nothing about the data changes, but the slope becomes a distribution, about which we can make direct statements of probability, and the dependence of the years of a country, which the CR2 test repairs after the fit, has to be written into the model itself. We take the steps in the order of the Bayesian workflow. First the priors and what they imply before the data enter, then the posterior of the two-way slope and the checks that its computation worked. Then the model fails a check against the data, and we take two readings of the failure: errors that persist within a country, and partial pooling, which gives every country a slope of its own. Last, the sensitivity to the priors, and the slope across all the models. The models take a while to fit, so they were fitted once, and the slides read their results.
:::
